section.title: The Trial, Crucifixion, and Burial
section.sectionRationale: Handed to Pilate and shuttled to Herod, Jesus is repeatedly declared innocent, yet the crowd demands Barabbas and cries for crucifixion until Pilate yields. On the way He tells the weeping women to weep for themselves, and at the Skull He is crucified between two criminals, praying, Father, forgive them. A dying thief believes and is promised Paradise. Darkness falls, the temple veil is torn, and Jesus commits His Spirit to the Father and dies. A centurion glorifies God, and Joseph of Arimathea lays Him in a new tomb as the Sabbath begins.
section.thesis: The innocent Son goes to the cross in the place of the guilty, forgiving His killers, opening Paradise to a dying thief, tearing the veil that barred the way to God, and entrusting His Spirit to the Father, so that His death is the innocent dying for the guilty and the way to God flung open.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the trials before Pilate and Herod; the choice of Barabbas and the sentence; the way to the cross and the daughters of Jerusalem; the crucifixion and the penitent criminal; the death of Jesus with the torn veil; and the burial by Joseph of Arimathea.

units.label: Before Pilate and Herod
units.note: I find no basis for a charge against this man

verses.text: Then the whole council rose and led Jesus away to Pilate.
And they began to accuse Him, saying, “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar, and proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King.”
So Pilate asked Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied.
Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no basis for a charge against this man.”
But they kept insisting, “He stirs up the people all over Judea with His teaching. He began in Galilee and has come all the way here.”
When Pilate heard this, he asked if the man was a Galilean.
And learning that Jesus was under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent Him to Herod, who himself was in Jerusalem at that time.
When Herod saw Jesus, he was greatly pleased. He had wanted to see Him for a long time, because he had heard about Him and was hoping to see Him perform a miracle.
Herod questioned Jesus at great length, but He gave no answer.
Meanwhile, the chief priests and scribes stood there, vehemently accusing Him.
And even Herod and his soldiers ridiculed and mocked Him. Dressing Him in a fine robe, they sent Him back to Pilate.
That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies.

units.label: Barabbas and the sentence
units.note: he handed Jesus over to their will

verses.text: Then Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people,
and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was inciting the people to rebellion. I have examined Him here in your presence and found Him not guilty of your charges against Him.
Neither has Herod, for he sent Him back to us. As you can see, He has done nothing deserving of death.
Therefore I will punish Him and release Him.”
But they all cried out in unison: “Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!”
(Barabbas had been imprisoned for an insurrection in the city, and for murder.)
Wanting to release Jesus, Pilate addressed them again,
but they kept shouting, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!”
A third time he said to them, “What evil has this man done? I have found in Him no offense worthy of death. So after I punish Him, I will release Him.”
But they were insistent, demanding with loud voices for Jesus to be crucified. And their clamor prevailed.
So Pilate sentenced that their demand be met.
As they had requested, he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and he handed Jesus over to their will.

units.label: The way to the cross
units.note: do not weep for Me, but for yourselves

verses.text: As the soldiers led Him away, they seized Simon of Cyrene on his way in from the country, and they put the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.
A great number of people followed Him, including women who kept mourning and wailing for Him.
But Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
Look, the days are coming when people will say, ‘Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!’
At that time ‘they will say to the mountains, “Fall on us!” and to the hills, “Cover us!”’
For if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?”

units.label: The crucifixion and the penitent criminal
units.note: today you will be with Me in Paradise

verses.text: Two others, who were criminals, were also led away to be executed with Jesus.
When they came to the place called The Skull, they {{stauroo|crucified}} Him there, along with the criminals, one on His right and the other on His left.
Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.
The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered at Him, saying, “He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One.”
The soldiers also mocked Him and came up to offer Him sour wine.
“If You are the King of the Jews,” they said, “save Yourself!”
Above Him was posted an inscription: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
One of the criminals who hung there heaped abuse on Him. “Are You not the Christ?” he said. “Save Yourself and us!”
But the other one rebuked him, saying, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment?
We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong.”
Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!”
And Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in {{paradeisos|Paradise}}.”

units.label: The death of Jesus
units.note: Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit

verses.text: It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour.
The sun was darkened, and the {{katapetasma|veil}} of the temple was torn down the middle.
Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I {{paratithemi|commit}} My Spirit.” And when He had said this, He breathed His last.
When the centurion saw what had happened, he gave glory to God, saying, “Surely this was a righteous man.”
And when all the people who had gathered for this spectacle saw what had happened, they returned home beating their breasts.
But all those who knew Jesus, including the women who had followed Him from Galilee, stood at a distance watching these things.

units.label: The burial of Jesus
units.note: a new tomb, where no one had yet been laid

verses.text: Now there was a Council member named Joseph, a good and righteous man,
who had not consented to their decision or action. He was from the Judean town of Arimathea and was waiting for the kingdom of God.
He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus.
Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and placed it in a tomb cut into the rock, where no one had yet been laid.
It was Preparation Day, and the Sabbath was beginning.
The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed, and they saw the tomb and how His body was placed.
Then they returned to prepare spices and perfumes. And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.

stauroo.gloss: To crucify, to put to death on a cross. The most shameful and agonizing of Roman executions, reserved for slaves and rebels, becomes the means of the world's salvation. The King of the Jews is crucified between two criminals, numbered with transgressors, bearing in His body the curse that fell on sinners.

paradeisos.gloss: Paradise, a garden of blessing, the presence of God. Jesus promises the dying, believing thief that this very day he will be with Him in Paradise. Salvation comes by simple faith at the last hour, apart from any works, and the assurance is immediate: to be with Christ is Paradise itself.

katapetasma.gloss: The veil, the great curtain that shut off the Most Holy Place. At the moment of Jesus' death it is torn down the middle, signaling that the barrier between God and sinners is removed. Through the torn body of Christ a new and living way into God's presence is opened for all who believe.

paratithemi.gloss: To entrust, to commit into another's keeping. Quoting Psalm 31, Jesus dies not in despair but in trust, committing His Spirit into the Father's hands. Even in death He is the faithful Son, entrusting Himself to the God who will raise Him, a pattern of trust for all who die in Him.

basic.context: The council brings Jesus to Pilate, charging Him with subversion and claiming to be a king. Pilate finds no guilt and sends Him to Herod, who mocks Him and sends Him back. Three times Pilate declares Him innocent, yet the crowd demands the release of Barabbas, a murderer, and shouts for Jesus to be crucified until Pilate gives in. On the way, Jesus tells the wailing women to weep for themselves and their city. At the Skull He is crucified between two criminals and prays, Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. The rulers, soldiers, and one criminal mock Him, but the other criminal believes and is promised, today you will be with Me in Paradise. Darkness falls, the temple veil is torn, and Jesus commits His Spirit to the Father and dies. A centurion praises God, and Joseph of Arimathea lays Him in a new tomb as the Sabbath begins.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the whole trial and crucifixion through Luke's insistence on Jesus' innocence: Pilate, Herod, the penitent thief, and the centurion all testify He has done nothing wrong. The innocent One dies in the place of the guilty, symbolized by Barabbas released and the thief forgiven, and the torn veil declares the way to God now open through His death.
basic.originalLanguages: The King is stauroo, crucified, the shameful death of rebels. To the believing thief He promises paradeisos, Paradise, that very day. At His death the katapetasma, the temple veil, is torn open. And He dies in trust, quoting Psalm 31, as He paratithemi, entrusts, His Spirit to the Father.
basic.typology: Barabbas the guilty released while the innocent dies pictures substitution, the sinner freed because Christ takes his place. The torn veil fulfills the tabernacle's barrier, now opened. The darkness and the righteous sufferer echo Psalm 22 and the prophets, and Jesus is the true Passover Lamb slain as the feast begins.
basic.christ: Jesus is the innocent King crucified for the guilty, who forgives His killers and opens Paradise to a dying thief. He is the true sacrifice whose death tears the veil, and the faithful Son who dies entrusting His Spirit to the Father, the righteous man the centurion confesses.
basic.god: God's saving purpose stands even through corrupt courts and a manipulated crowd. God accepts the innocent in place of the guilty, opens the way to His presence through the torn veil, and receives the Spirit of His trusting Son. His justice and mercy meet at the cross.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53 foretells the innocent servant who bears the sin of many. Psalm 22 is the psalm of the mocked, pierced sufferer whose garments are divided. Psalm 31 supplies the dying words, into Your hands I commit My spirit. Hebrews 10 explains the torn veil as the new way into God's presence.
basic.oneStory: At the cross the innocent Son dies for the guilty, the barrier to God is torn away, and a dying criminal enters Paradise by faith alone. The story reaches its darkest and brightest point together: the Lamb is slain, the veil is opened, and the trusting Son is laid in a tomb, waiting for the dawn of resurrection.

context.literary:
Luke 23 is built around a single repeated verdict. Three times Pilate says Jesus is innocent: 'I find no basis for a charge against this man,' verse 4, 'found Him not guilty,' verse 14, and 'I have found in Him no offense worthy of death,' verse 22. Herod, in verse 15, joins the testimony by sending Him back. The condemned man is the one whom every legal authority in the story has declared blameless. Then, at the cross, the verdict is taken up by a criminal, 'this man has done nothing wrong,' verse 41, and by a centurion, 'Surely this was a righteous man,' verse 47. The innocence of Jesus runs through the chapter like a thread, from the governor's mouth to the thief's to the soldier's.

The chapter moves in two panels. The first, verses 1 to 25, is a courtroom, which grows steadily louder: the charge in verse 2, the transfers to Herod and back, and then the crowd's shouting that finally 'prevailed,' verse 23. The second, verses 26 to 56, is slower, in which the human voices of mockery are arranged in three tiers: the rulers, the soldiers, and the criminal, verses 35 to 39. Each mocks with the same words, 'save Yourself,' and each is answered not by a defence but by the one who actually saves, the other criminal. The theme of 'save' is what the chapter turns on.

Luke builds a careful sequence at the death itself. Darkness comes from the sixth to the ninth hour, the veil is torn, Jesus cries out in a loud voice and breathes His last, verses 44 to 46, and Luke makes three reactions follow: the centurion glorifies God, the crowds return beating their breasts, and the acquaintances and the women stand at a distance, verses 47 to 49. The chapter then moves from death to burial in order: Joseph's request, the linen cloth, the new tomb, the women who see 'how His body was placed,' and the Sabbath, verses 50 to 56. Everything is arranged to prepare for the empty tomb of chapter 24, as the women who watched the burial will be the first to find it empty.
context.historical:
Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea, appointed under Tiberius, Luke 3:1. He alone held the power of execution in a province like this, and the leaders needed him for that reason. The charges of verse 2 are carefully political, since a Roman governor would not care about a theological dispute: subverting the nation, forbidding tax to Caesar, and claiming to be a king. Luke has just shown that the tax charge is false, Luke 20:25. The question 'Are You the King of the Jews?' is the only one Pilate asks, because kingship was the sort of claim that could threaten Rome.

Herod Antipas ruled Galilee, verse 7, and was in Jerusalem for the feast. Luke 9:9 had said he wanted to see Jesus, and the wish is fulfilled here with no result. The fine robe of verse 11 is a mock royal garment. That Herod and Pilate became friends that day, verse 12, reveals the sort of alliance a common enemy can make, and Acts 4:27 later reads it as the fulfilment of Psalm 2.

Crucifixion was Rome's execution for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals. Simon of Cyrene, a Jew from North Africa in Jerusalem for the feast, is pressed into carrying the cross beam, as a Roman soldier could compel a local to carry a load. The women in verses 27 to 28 were mourners, and the practice of mourning for the condemned was kept even under Roman rule. The place called The Skull, verse 33, lay outside the walls. The division of clothing was the executioners' customary share. The drink of sour wine, verse 36, was the soldiers' cheap wine.

Under Jewish law a body hung on a tree could not stay overnight, Deuteronomy 21:22 to 23, which is why Joseph, a member of the council who had not agreed to the decision, asked Pilate for the body before the Sabbath began. A rock-cut tomb in which no one had yet been laid belonged to a man of means, and the burial, hurried by the setting sun, left the spices for the women to prepare after the rest.
context.canonical:
The cross of Luke 23 fulfils texts across the Old Testament, and the chapter echoes them without always naming them. Three psalms are heard most clearly. Psalm 22 stands behind the dividing of garments, verse 34, the sneering of the people, verse 35, and the cry that follows. The footnotes of the BSB mark Psalm 22:18 and 22:7 at verses 34 and 35. Psalm 69:21, 'they gave me vinegar to quench my thirst,' lies behind the sour wine of verse 36. And Jesus' last words are Psalm 31:5, 'Into Your hands I commit my spirit,' the footnote at verse 46.

Isaiah 53 is the chapter's prophetic frame. The Servant 'was numbered with the transgressors' and 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, and 'was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death,' Isaiah 53:9. Luke gives the transgressors on either side, and a rich man, Joseph, who gives the tomb. The women's grief draws on Hosea 10:8, 'Then they will say to the mountains, "Cover us!" and to the hills, "Fall on us!"' the footnote at verse 30, which Revelation 6:16 applies to the final judgment. The 'green' and 'dry' tree of verse 31 may recall Ezekiel 20:47 and 17:24.

The New Testament comments on the cross with great regularity. Peter says that the people 'rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you,' Acts 3:14, and calls the cross a tree, Acts 5:30, in the language of Deuteronomy 21:23, which Paul connects to Christ in Galatians 3:13: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.' The torn veil is interpreted in Hebrews, 'the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:20. And the promise of Paradise is picked up in 2 Corinthians 12:4 and Revelation 2:7, where the tree of life is in the Paradise of God, drawing the line right back to Eden.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke is writing to people who might hear that the founder of the Christian movement was executed as a criminal and wonder if they have trusted the wrong man. He answers by assembling witnesses to innocence. The governor, the tetrarch, the criminal beside Him and the centurion all say so. This was not a justice that went wrong because Jesus was guilty. It went wrong because He was not, and that made the cross a different kind of event: the righteous one in the place of the guilty.

At the same time Luke wants his readers to see that nothing here is accidental. The same Peter who tells the crowds that they killed the Author of life also says that God had foretold it, Acts 3:15 and 3:18. The cry of the crowd prevails, and yet Jesus goes to the cross as the one who has said, 'Into Your hands I commit My Spirit.' Luke writes in such a way that human guilt and divine purpose are both true.

He also writes to form his readers. The prayer 'Father, forgive them' is meant to shape how Christians treat their enemies, and Stephen's prayer in Acts 7:60 is its echo. The promise to the thief is meant to assure every late and unlikely believer. The torn veil and the stepping forward of Joseph show that the death of Jesus makes bold access and bold loyalty possible.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The crucifixion is narrated as the once-for-all saving death of Christ, which no one repeats and no one improves. We do not copy what Jesus does on the cross, such as bearing sin, but we trust it. What is prescriptive in the chapter comes in the form of examples that Luke draws out. The prayer of forgiveness for one's killers is a pattern that Stephen follows and that the New Testament commends, as in 1 Peter 2:23. Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross 'behind Jesus' is described, but Luke has twice used the same picture for discipleship, Luke 9:23 and 14:27, so that it becomes a picture of what following Him involves.

The penitent thief is a description of how one man was saved at the end of his life, and it is not a rule that a believer may put off repentance. Luke 23:43 is also not a general lesson on the afterlife, though it says something about it: to be with Christ is Paradise.

The behaviour of the others is a warning and not a pattern: the leaders who sneer, the soldiers who mock, Pilate who gives in against his own judgment, the crowd that shouts. The women who weep are told to weep for themselves, and the instruction applies more widely. Sympathy at the sight of Jesus' suffering is not the same as repentance.

debates.question: What does the promise of Paradise to the thief teach about salvation?

views.label: Salvation by grace through faith alone, apart from works
views.case: The thief can do nothing but believe and appeal to Jesus; he has no time for baptism, penance, or good works, yet Jesus assures him of Paradise that very day. The scene displays justification by faith at the eleventh hour, resting wholly on Christ and His grace.

views.label: The immediate blessedness of being with Christ after death
views.case: The word 'today' also teaches that the believer is with Christ at once upon death; there is no long sleep or delay before entering His presence. To die in faith is to be with the Lord in Paradise immediately, a comfort for all who trust Him.

debates.bearing: Both truths stand together: the dying thief is saved by faith alone in the crucified King, and to be with Christ, that very day, is Paradise, so no repentant sinner who turns to Jesus is ever too late.

debates.question: What does the tearing of the temple veil signify?

views.label: The opening of the way into God's presence
views.case: The veil barred access to the Most Holy Place; its tearing at Jesus' death declares that through His sacrifice the barrier between God and sinners is removed, and all who come by faith may now draw near. Hebrews reads it exactly this way, a new and living way opened through His flesh.

views.label: A sign of judgment on the temple and its order
views.case: The torn veil can also signal that the temple's day is ending, its holiness exposed and its function fulfilled, as Jesus becomes the true meeting place with God and the temple faces the destruction He foretold. The sign points both to open access and to the passing of the old order.

debates.bearing: Whether stressing access or judgment, the torn veil proclaims that through the death of Christ the old barrier is gone and God is now approached through the crucified Son.

study.originalLanguages:
Pilate says in verse 16 that he will 'punish' Jesus and release Him, using paideuo, which is the verb of discipline and training and here means a flogging as a warning. The word is gentle in its ordinary use and chilling here. Pilate also repeats the verb apoluo, 'release,' in verses 16, 18, 20 and 22, in a series that the crowd answers with a different word, 'Away with this man!' In verse 25 Luke says Pilate 'handed Jesus over to their will,' to thelemati auton. In the garden Jesus had prayed 'not My will, but Yours,' the same word thelema, Luke 22:42. Two wills are in the scene: the will of the crowd that Pilate follows, and the will of the Father that Jesus follows, and the second governs the first.

The name Barabbas is Aramaic, bar abba, 'son of the father.' The man who is released is a 'son of the father' who had committed insurrection and murder, and the one who dies in his place is the Son of the Father in a fuller sense. Luke does not make a point of this, but the name is there for those who can hear it.

Simon is made to carry the cross 'behind Jesus,' opisthen tou Iesou. Luke uses the same adverb of discipleship in Luke 14:27, where the one who will not carry his cross and come 'after Me' cannot be His disciple. In verse 31 the 'tree' that is green or dry is xylon, 'wood,' the word used of the cross in Acts 5:30 and in the Greek translation of Deuteronomy 21:23. The saying is an argument from the lesser to the greater: if this is done to the innocent, what awaits the guilty city?

Verse 34 has a prayer that is hard to translate in a smooth rhythm: aphes autois, ou gar oidasin ti poiousin, 'forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' The verb aphiemi is the word for sending away or releasing, and the ordinary word for forgiveness in Luke. As the footnote says, some manuscripts do not include the prayer, though its place in the earliest tradition is generally accepted, and Acts 3:17 and 1 Corinthians 2:8 speak of the rulers' ignorance in a way that matches it.

The rulers 'sneered,' exemykterizon, a verb that means to turn up the nose in contempt. They call Him 'the Christ of God, the Chosen One,' ho eklektos, titles they mean sarcastically and which are exactly true. The soldiers 'mocked,' enepaixan, a word of play and ridicule. Three times the same words are used, 'save Yourself.' The chapter's irony is that He does save, but not Himself.

The penitent says, 'remember me,' mnestheti mou, a request that echoes the many Old Testament prayers that ask God to remember. Jesus answers with 'Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise,' with 'today,' semeron, a word Luke has used before for the arrival of salvation, as in Luke 19:9, and with 'with Me,' met' emou, which is more than the man asked. He asked to be remembered at a future kingdom, and he is given company that very day.

In verse 45 the sun was 'darkened,' and the footnote says the verb may also mean failed or was obscured, which is the verb ekleipo, the root of 'eclipse.' The veil 'was torn down the middle,' eschisthe meson. Luke tells of the tearing before Jesus' death, while Matthew and Mark put it at the death. He is not contradicting them. His order places the opening of God's presence at the start of the final act. The loud voice, phone megale, and the verb for 'breathed His last,' exepneusen, show a death that is a deliberate release.

The centurion calls Him dikaios, 'righteous,' and the BSB footnote gives 'innocent' as another rendering. Both are true, since the word covers a man who is upright and a man who is in the right. Acts 3:14 later calls Jesus 'the Holy and Righteous One,' using the same word. And the crowds who came for the 'spectacle,' theoria, go home beating their breasts, a spectacle they had come to see turning on them.

typology.fulfillment: A man guilty of insurrection and murder goes free and the innocent one is condemned. It is the clearest picture in the narrative of substitution, and Luke tells it in the plainest terms: 'he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and handed Jesus over to their will.' Barabbas is a type of every sinner who is let go because another is taken. Paul gives the doctrine: 'While we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8, and Peter, 'the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God,' 1 Peter 3:18. The type falls short because Barabbas does not know what has happened, whereas believers are called to know and trust it.

typology.type: The veil of the sanctuary, Exodus 26:31 to 33
typology.fulfillment: The veil, woven with cherubim, hung to 'separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place,' Exodus 26:31 to 33, so that only the high priest passed behind it once a year. At the death of Jesus it is torn down the middle, verse 45. Hebrews says that believers may now enter the Most Holy Place 'by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19 to 20. The escalation is from one man entering once a year with the blood of animals to all God's people drawing near through one sacrifice. The type is fulfilled and not simply removed: the veil's meaning of separation by sin is dealt with.

typology.type: Darkness over the land, Exodus 10:22 and Amos 8:9
typology.fulfillment: At the sixth hour darkness covers all the land until the ninth, verse 44. In Egypt a thick darkness fell on the land as judgment before the Passover, Exodus 10:22, and Amos had said that on the day of the LORD God would 'make the sun go down at noon,' Amos 8:9. The darkness at the cross carries the signs of judgment: God's verdict falls on sin at the very place where His Son bears it. It points to the same darkness that Jesus called 'the power of darkness' in Luke 22:53. The sign is partial because the darkness lasts three hours and ends in light, as the resurrection will be.

typology.type: The one hung on a tree, Deuteronomy 21:22 to 23
typology.fulfillment: The law said that anyone hanged on a tree was under God's curse and must be buried that day. Joseph's rush to bury Jesus before the Sabbath begins, verses 50 to 54, honours that law without knowing its full meaning. Paul spells it out: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The shameful death that looked like proof of God's rejection was the means by which the curse was borne. The correspondence is complete but one-sided: the curse He took was ours, and He had done nothing to deserve it.

typology.type: The righteous sufferer of the psalms, Psalm 22 and Psalm 31
typology.fulfillment: David's psalms of the righteous man mocked and surrounded give Luke's scene its words: the divided garments, the sneers, and the final trust of Psalm 31:5, 'Into Your hands I commit my spirit.' Jesus takes the psalms of the righteous sufferer on His lips and lives them out. He is what David could describe only in part. In the psalms the sufferer is delivered from his troubles, while here He is delivered through death by resurrection, and the psalms end in praise that reaches the nations, which the resurrection opens.

study.christ:
Luke leads to Christ here by presenting Him as the innocent one. Every verdict in the chapter agrees, and the agreement is intentional. Peter will say later that the rulers 'rejected the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14, and Paul that 'they found no ground for a death sentence,' Acts 13:28. Jesus is not a victim of a miscarriage that God failed to foresee. He is the righteous one who stands in the place of the unrighteous. 'Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God,' 1 Peter 3:18.

He is the King. The inscription, 'THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS,' is meant as mockery and is true. Every word spoken against Him confirms His identity: the Christ, the Chosen One, the King. The crown is a cross, and the throne is a tree. Yet it is exactly here that He is made to reign, for the thief who asks about His kingdom is given Paradise.

He is the Saviour who does not save Himself. 'He saved others; let Him save Himself,' the rulers say. The sentence is accurate in its first half and blind in its second. He saved others by not saving Himself. Simeon in Luke 2 was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the two travellers to Emmaus will say, 'we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel,' Luke 24:21. The redemption happens where they least expected it.

He is the forgiver. 'Father, forgive them' is spoken while the nails are being driven and the lots cast. The prayer of the Servant who 'made intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12, is answered in the lives of those who will later repent at Pentecost and be told, 'you acted in ignorance,' Acts 3:17. Forgiveness is not a reward for the worthy but a gift from the cross itself.

He is the one who opens Paradise. To the thief He says, 'today you will be with Me in Paradise.' The man's whole claim is that Jesus has a kingdom, and the King's answer is that where He is, is Paradise. Paradise reaches back to Eden and forward to the tree of life in the Paradise of God, Revelation 2:7. He restores what the first Adam lost.

He is the new way into the presence of God. The tearing of the veil announces that what the sanctuary guarded is now open, Hebrews 10:19 to 20. The curtain is His body, and by His broken body the way is open.

He is the Son who trusts. 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit' is Psalm 31:5, a psalm of trust spoken by a man in danger, now made the last word of a life. The Son who began the night saying 'Not My will, but Yours' ends the day committing Himself, in perfect trust, to the Father who seems far away. He is a model for dying, but first He is the one who dies for us, the Lamb who was bound and offered. Hebrews 9:26 sums it up: He has appeared 'once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.'

A caution keeps the reading honest. The fine robe, the sour wine, Simon's burden and the linen cloth are real details, and they do not each hide a hidden doctrine. The chapter's meaning is carried by Jesus' words and by what the narrator says about innocence, forgiveness, access and trust.
study.god:
The cross shows God to be just. It is no sentimental forgiveness that overlooks wrong. Paul says that God 'presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness,' so as 'to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:25 to 26. The darkness, the torn veil and the cry of verse 46 belong to a God who takes sin seriously enough that the sacrifice is His own Son. Justice is not set aside at the cross but fulfilled.

He is merciful. In the same scene the Son prays for His killers and promises Paradise to a convicted man who has only a few hours to live. The mercy is not bought by any quality in the thief, who brings nothing but a confession and a request. Here the sinner needs only to ask. A God who gives such an answer to such a prayer is the God Jesus described in the parable of the lost son.

He is sovereign over the wickedness of men. Pilate caves, the crowd shouts, the rulers sneer, and yet Peter says that this was by God's set plan, Acts 2:23, and the prayer in Acts 4:27 to 28 says that Herod and Pilate carried out what God's hand had decided beforehand. This does not excuse them. The text insists they acted in ignorance but also that they were responsible. God rules without being the author of their evil, and He turns the worst deed in history to the best end.

He is a God who stays near even when He seems far away. The darkness and the silence are real, and the Son does not cry out in answer but in trust. The Father's nearness is not shown by the removal of the pain but by the confidence of the cry, 'Father, into Your hands.' The tearing of the veil answers in action what the darkness conceals: God is not driving people away but opening the way.

He is holy. The veil was there for centuries to say that sinners may not approach, and its tearing does not say that holiness has been relaxed. It says that holiness has been satisfied. The one who tears it is God, not man, and it is torn from the top down in the other accounts, an act of God's own initiative.

He keeps faith with His promises. The women watch the burial, and the Sabbath is observed 'according to the commandment.' Everything is placed in readiness for the third day that Jesus had promised, Luke 18:33. The God who permitted the cross is the God who will raise the body that Joseph laid in the rock.

Worship in this light is gratitude and awe: gratitude that the Judge Himself bore the sentence, and awe that He did it for people who knew not what they did. It also gives us a language for dying well, as Jesus did, and for praying for those who wrong us.

crossReferences.note: The Servant 'was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.' Luke shows two criminals beside Him and a rich councillor, Joseph, who gives the tomb. The prophecy fits both the company at the cross and the place of burial.

The psalm of the righteous sufferer contains the mocking crowds, 'He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him,' the pierced hands and feet, and the division of garments by lot. Luke's footnotes mark verses 7 and 18. The whole scene is told with its words, and the psalm's final turn to praise points on to the resurrection.

'Into Your hands I commit my spirit; You have redeemed me.' Jesus' last words are the first line of a psalm of trust spoken by a man in danger. He adds the word 'Father,' and the whole cross becomes an act of trust in the God who will redeem.

'They will say to the mountains, "Cover us!" and to the hills, "Fall on us!"' Jesus applies the verse to the coming judgment on Jerusalem in verse 30, and Revelation 6:16 uses it for the final judgment. Hosea's judgment on false worship becomes a warning about rejecting the Messiah.

The law that a hanged man is under God's curse and must be buried before nightfall explains Joseph's haste and the meaning of the shame. Paul uses it in Galatians 3:13 to show that Christ bore the curse. The cross is the place where law's curse and God's grace meet.

Believers may enter the Most Holy Place 'by the blood of Jesus,' through 'the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body.' It is the New Testament's own reading of the torn veil, showing that Luke 23:45 means open access and not merely judgment.

Peter charges the people with handing Jesus over and rejecting Him before Pilate, who had decided to release Him, and with asking for a murderer in His place. It is a summary of the chapter's courtroom, and the same speech says God raised the 'Author of life.'

Stephen, dying under stones, prays 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them,' and falls asleep. His prayer is a deliberate echo of 'Father, forgive them,' and shows the death of Jesus reshaping how His followers die.

'Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.' This is a compact commentary on Luke's emphasis on innocence and on the Barabbas exchange, saying what the innocent death accomplished.

The overcomer will eat from the tree of life 'in the Paradise of God.' Jesus' promise to the thief, 'in Paradise,' is thereby linked to the garden of Eden and the tree of life, so that the criminal's hope is the final restoration of what was lost.

John adds that Nicodemus brought myrrh and aloes and that the tomb was in a garden. It fills out Luke's brief account of the burial, confirms the 'new tomb in which no one had yet been laid,' and sets the burial in a garden, as the story began.

'While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.' Paul states in one line what Luke shows in Barabbas, the thief and the centurion: the death of Jesus is for the guilty and the ungodly, and that is the measure of God's love.

study.oneStory:
The cross is where the story's two long lines meet. One line is the curse that fell in Eden: the ground, the tree, exile from the garden and the cherubim at the gate. The other is the promise to Abraham, that in his seed the nations would be blessed, and to Israel's king, whose throne would last forever. On the cross the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23 is borne by the seed, and the blessing begins to flow out. Paul says that He became a curse so that 'the blessing of Abraham' might come to the nations, Galatians 3:13 and 3:14.

The chapter also answers the question that the whole sacrificial system asked. For centuries priests offered animals behind a veil that no one else could pass. The system pointed beyond itself to a better sacrifice and an open way. At the moment of His death the veil is torn, the centurion, a Gentile, glorifies God, and a thief is promised Paradise. All of this shows who the new people will be: those who come not by pedigree or merit but by a cry to Jesus.

Within Luke the cross answers the opening promises. Simeon waited for the consolation of Israel, Luke 2:25, and the Emmaus travellers hoped for redemption, Luke 24:21. What they wanted is accomplished in the way they did not expect. The burial leads on to the Sabbath rest and then the first day, chapter 24, where Jesus will say that it was written that the Christ would suffer and rise and that repentance and forgiveness would be preached to all nations, Luke 24:46 to 47.

The story ends in the new creation, where the thief's Paradise is fully revealed. The tree of life is back, the curse is gone, and there is no temple because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22 and 22:3. The veil that was torn at Golgotha will not be needed again. The King whom they mocked will reign, and the people who were forgiven by His prayer will see His face. Between the cross and that day, the church lives by the three sentences spoken here: Father, forgive them; today you will be with Me; Father, into Your hands.

quiz.q: What verdict do Pilate and Herod reach about Jesus?

options.text: That He is innocent, having done nothing deserving of death.
options.note: Luke 23:4,14-15,22 repeatedly declares Jesus not guilty.

options.text: That the charges against Him were unproven.
options.note: True, but weaker than Luke's repeated, emphatic declaration of His innocence.

options.text: That He was guilty but did not deserve death.
options.note: They find no guilt at all, not merely a lesser guilt.

options.text: That He was clearly guilty of inciting rebellion.
options.note: The opposite: they find no basis for the charge of rebellion.

quiz.q: What happens when the crowd is given a choice?

options.text: They demand the release of Barabbas, a murderer, and the crucifixion of the innocent Jesus.
options.note: Luke 23:18-25 shows the guilty freed and the innocent condemned.

options.text: They call for Jesus to be crucified.
options.note: True, but it omits the pointed contrast of Barabbas the murderer set free in His place.

options.text: They ask Pilate to decide for himself.
options.note: They actively demand Barabbas and shout for crucifixion, not a neutral deferral.

options.text: They ask for both men to be released.
options.note: They demand Barabbas released and Jesus crucified.

quiz.q: How does Jesus respond to the penitent criminal?

options.text: He promises, today you will be with Me in Paradise, saving him by faith alone at the last hour.
options.note: Luke 23:43 assures the believing thief of immediate Paradise.

options.text: He assures the man that he will be remembered in the kingdom.
options.note: True to the man's request, but Jesus promises far more: Paradise that very day.

options.text: He tells the man to prove his repentance by his deeds.
options.note: The thief can do no works; he is saved by faith alone, not by proving himself.

options.text: He remains silent to the criminal's plea.
options.note: Jesus answers with a direct promise of Paradise.

quiz.q: What happens at the moment of Jesus' death?

options.text: Darkness covers the land, the temple veil is torn, and Jesus commits His Spirit to the Father.
options.note: Luke 23:44-46 records the darkness, the torn veil, and His trusting last words.

options.text: Jesus cries out and breathes His last.
options.note: True, but it omits the darkness and the torn veil that interpret His death.

options.text: Jesus dies quietly with no accompanying signs.
options.note: There are dramatic signs: darkness and the tearing of the veil.

options.text: The temple is immediately destroyed.
options.note: The veil is torn, not the temple destroyed; that judgment comes later.

quiz.q: What does the tearing of the temple veil signify?

options.text: The barrier between God and sinners is removed, opening the way into His presence through Christ's death.
options.note: The torn veil declares open access to God, as Hebrews 10 explains.

options.text: The old temple order is passing away.
options.note: True as a secondary sense, but the primary meaning is the opened way into God's presence.

options.text: The temple curtain was simply worn out.
options.note: The tearing is a divine sign tied to Jesus' death, not natural wear.

options.text: God had abandoned His people entirely.
options.note: The opposite: the way to God is now thrown open through Christ.

questions: Barabbas the guilty walked free because the innocent Jesus took his place. How does it change you to see yourself in Barabbas, released because Christ was condemned?
From the cross Jesus prayed, Father, forgive them. Is there someone you consider beyond forgiveness, and how does His prayer confront your own unforgiveness?
The dying thief was saved with no time for works, only faith. Does that comfort you or unsettle you, and what does it say about how anyone is saved?
The veil was torn so you could come near to God. Do you live as one shut out, or as one welcomed freely into His presence through Christ?
Jesus died entrusting His Spirit to the Father. What would it mean for you to face your fears, and finally death itself, with that same trust?

translationNotes.note: The BSB omits verse 17, moving from verse 16 to 18, because the earliest manuscripts do not contain it. Some later manuscripts add, 'Now Pilate was obligated to release to the people one prisoner at the feast,' drawn from Matthew 27:15 and Mark 15:6. The custom it describes is still evident in the crowd's demand for Barabbas.

Some manuscripts do not include 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' The BSB retains this well-loved saying, which fits Luke's portrait of Jesus praying for His enemies even from the cross.
Jesus' dying words quote Psalm 31:5, 'Into Your hand I commit my spirit.' He dies not in despair but in trust, entrusting Himself to the Father who will raise Him.
